1.o: The narrative which this evangelist gives us (or rather God by him) of the life of Christ begins earlier than either Matthew or Mark. We have reason to thank God for them all, as we have for all the gifts and graces of Christ's ministers, which in one make up what is wanting in the other, while all put together make a harmony. In this chapter we have, I. Luke's preface to his gospel, or his epistle dedicatory to his friend Theophilus, ver. 1-4. II.
1.i: A priest named Zechariah is chosen to burn incense in the Temple, where an angel tells him his wife will have a son, John.
1.p: Lord, You remember Your people. Give us patience to wait and faith to believe when You answer. Amen.
1.l: Pray for something you have waited a long time for, and trust that God hears you.
q: Zechariah had prayed for years. How do you keep praying when the answer seems far away?

2.o: In this chapter, we have an account of the birth and infancy of our Lord Jesus: having had notice of his conception, and of the birth and infancy of his forerunner, in the former chapter. The First-begotten is here brought into the world; let us go meet him with our hosannas, blessed is he that cometh. Here is, I. The place and other circumstances of his birth, which proved him to be the true Messiah, and such a one as we needed, but not such a one as the Jews expected, ver. 1-7. II.
2.i: Jesus is born in Bethlehem, angels sing to shepherds, and the shepherds find the baby in a manger.
2.p: Lord Jesus, You were born for us. We thank You and praise You for the good news. Amen.
2.l: Tell someone the good news today, in your own words, that Jesus was born.
q: God told the shepherds first. What does that tell you about whom Jesus came for?

3.o: Nothing is related concerning our Lord Jesus from his twelfth year to his entrance on his thirtieth year. We often think it would have been a pleasure and advantage to us if we had journals, or at least annuls, of occurrences concerning him; but we have as much as Infinite Wisdom thought fit to communicate to us, and, if we improve not that, neither should we have improved more if we had had it.
3.i: John the Baptist preached repentance in the wilderness, told each group of listeners how to live honestly, and pointed to Jesus, the One coming after him.
3.p: Lord, make straight the road in our hearts for You. Teach us to share, to be honest, and to be content. Amen.
3.l: John said to share. Find something you have more than one of, and give one to someone who needs it.
q: John told ordinary people ordinary things to do. What is one ordinary change you need to make?

4.o: We left Christ newly baptized, and owned by a voice from heaven and the descent of the Holy Ghost upon him. Now, in this chapter, we have, I. A further preparation of him for his public ministry by his being tempted in the wilderness, of which we had the same account before in Matthew as we have here, ver. 1-13. II. His entrance upon his public work in Galilee (ver. 14, 15), particularly, 1. At Nazareth, the city where he had been bred up (ver. 16-30), which we had no account of before in Matthew. 2.
4.i: Jesus reads Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue, says it is fulfilled in him, and is driven out by an angry crowd.
4.p: Lord Jesus, You came to set captives free. Open our hearts to hear Your good news, even when it is hard. Amen.
4.l: Be kind to someone in your family or hometown who thinks they know you, and let your actions speak.
q: The people of Nazareth loved the gracious words, but were angry at the lesson. Which lessons are hard for you?

5.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ preaching to the people out of Peter's ship, for want of a better pulpit, ver. 1-3. II. The recompence he made to Peter for the loan of his boat, in a miraculous draught of fishes, by which he intimated to him and his partners his design to make them, as apostles, fishers of men, ver. 4-11. III. His cleansing the leper, ver. 12-15. IV. A short account of his private devotion and public ministry, ver. 16, 17. V. His cure of the man sick of the palsy, ver. 18-26. VI.
5.i: After a night of catching nothing, Peter obeyed Jesus and landed so many fish his boats nearly sank, and then he left everything to follow Jesus.
5.p: Lord Jesus, we are not worthy, but You call us anyway. Give us faith to launch out into the deep. Amen.
5.l: If someone asks you to do something that does not seem to make sense, do it with a good attitude today, because someone you trust asked.
q: Peter obeyed even when it did not make sense. What do you need to do because Jesus says so?

6.o: In this chapter we have Christ's exposition of the moral law, which he came not to destroy, but to fulfil, and to fill up, by his gospel. I. Here is a proof of the lawfulness of works of necessity and mercy on the sabbath day, the former in vindication of his disciples' plucking the ears of corn, the latter in vindication of himself healing the withered hand on that day, ver. 1-11. II. His retirement for secret prayer, ver. 12. III. His calling his twelve apostles, ver. 13-16. IV.
6.i: A cloak and a tunic were two different garments: the tunic a close-fitting shirt, the cloak a wool wrapper that was the poor man's bedding.
6.l: Do one good thing today for someone who has been unkind to you.
q: Be as ready to do good to an enemy as to anyone else. Who is the one you would help last?

7.o: In this chapter we have, I. Christ confirming the doctrine he had preached in the former chapter, with two glorious miracles—the curing of one at a distance, and that was the centurion's servant (ver. 1-10), and the raising of one to life that was dead, the widow's son at Nain, ver. 11-18. II. Christ confirming the faith of John who was now in prison, and of some of his disciples, by sending him a short account of the miracles he wrought, in answer to a question he received from him (ver.
7.i: A Roman officer said he was not worthy to have Jesus under his roof, yet trusted Jesus' word completely, and Jesus said He had not found faith like that anywhere in Israel.
7.p: Lord Jesus, You heal with a word. Give us the humble, plain trust of the centurion. Amen.
7.l: When you feel too small to ask God for something, ask anyway, the way the centurion did: humbly, and sure that He can do it.
q: The centurion trusted Jesus' word without needing to see it work first. Where do you want proof before you trust?

8.o: Most of this chapter is a repetition of divers passages of Christ's preaching and miracles which we had before in Matthew and Mark; they are all of such weight, that they are worth repeating, and therefore they are repeated, that out of the mouth not only of two, but of three, witnesses every word may be established. Here is, I. A general account of Christ's preaching, and how he had subsistence for himself and his numerous family by the charitable contributions of good people, ver. 1-3. II.
8.i: Women healed by Jesus, including Mary Magdalene and Joanna, travel with him and support his ministry.
8.p: Lord Jesus, You free and heal. Thank You for those who follow You with all they have. Amen.
8.l: Use something you have to help others today, such as your time, your lunch, or your skills.
q: These women gave their money and their time to support Jesus. What do you have that you can give?

9.o: In this chapter we have, I. The commission Christ gave to his twelve apostles to go out for some time to preach the gospel, and confirm it by miracles, ver. 1-6. II. Herod's terror at the growing greatness of our Lord Jesus, ver. 7-9. III. The apostles' return to Christ, his retirement with them into a place of solitude, the great resort of people to them notwithstanding, and his feeding five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, ver. 10-17. IV.
9.i: A boy's five barley loaves and two fish fed thousands once Jesus took them, thanked God, and gave them out in order.
9.p: Lord Jesus, You take small gifts and make them enough. Take what we have, and use it. Amen.
9.l: Share something small today, a snack, a toy, a few minutes of your time, and ask Jesus to make it enough.
q: The disciples saw only five loaves and two fish. What small thing could you put in Jesus' hands today?

10.o: In this chapter we have, I. The ample commission which Christ gave to the seventy disciples to preach the gospel, and to confirm it by miracles; and the full instructions he gave them how to manage themselves in the execution of their commissions, and great encouragements therein, ver. 1-16. II. The report which the seventy disciples made to their Master of the success of their negotiation, and his discourse thereupon, ver. 17-24. III.
10.s: The Man on the Jericho Road
10.i: Jesus answers a lawyer's question about who counts as a neighbor with a story set on a steep and dangerous road.
10.p: Lord Jesus, You showed us mercy when we were hurt and lost. Make us people who stop, see and help. Amen.
10.l: Notice someone who needs help today, and do one kind thing for them, even if you do not know them well.
q: Jesus turned who is my neighbor into who acts like a neighbor. Whom can you be a neighbor to today?

11.o: In this chapter, I. Christ teaches his disciples to pray, and quickens and encourages them to be frequent, instant, and importunate in prayer, ver. 1-13. II. He fully answers the blasphemous imputation of the Pharisees, who charged him with casting out devils by virtue of a compact and confederacy with Beelzebub, the prince of the devils, and shows the absurdity and wickedness of it, ver. 14-26. III. He shows the honour of obedient disciples to be greater than that of his own mother, ver. 27, 28. IV.
11.i: Why the disciples mentioned John: Jewish prayers were generally praises of God, and John had taught his disciples prayers full of petitions, according to Lightfoot.
11.l: Ask God today to teach you to pray, in your own words.
q: It is a hard thing to pray well. What would you ask Jesus to teach you about praying?

12.o: In this chapter we have divers excellent discourses of our Saviour's upon various occasions, many of which are to the same purport with what we had in Matthew upon other the like occasions; for we may suppose that our Lord Jesus preached the same doctrines, and pressed the same duties, at several times, in several companies, and that one of the evangelists took them as he delivered them at one time and another at another time; and we need thus to have precept upon precept, line upon line. Here, I.
12.s: The Rich Man's Barns and the Ravens
12.i: When a man asked Jesus to settle an inheritance, He told of a rich farmer who stored up goods and lost his life, and pointed his disciples to ravens that God feeds.
12.p: Lord, You feed the ravens and You feed us. Free us from greed and worry, and make us generous. Amen.
12.l: Give something away today, a toy, a snack, or an hour, and see how it feels to hold things loosely.
q: The farmer talked only to himself. Who do you talk to about what you have?

13.o: In this chapter we have, I. The good improvement Christ made of a piece of news that was brought him concerning some Galileans, that were lately massacred by Pilate, as they were sacrificing in the temple at Jerusalem, ver. 1-5. II. The parable of the fruitless fig-tree, by which we are warned to bring forth fruits meet for that repentance to which he had in the foregoing passage called us, ver. 6-9. III. Christ's healing a poor infirm woman on the sabbath day, and justifying himself in it, ver. 11-17. IV.
13.i: Jesus noticed a woman who had not asked for help, set her free on the Sabbath, and called her a daughter of Abraham.
13.p: Lord Jesus, You see those who do not ask. Set us free from whatever bends us down, and make us people who notice others. Amen.
13.l: Today, look up and notice someone who is usually overlooked. Say hello and use their name.
q: Jesus saw her before she asked. Who might He be asking you to notice before they ask for help?

14.o: In this chapter we have, I. The cure which our Lord Jesus wrought upon a man that had the dropsy, on the sabbath day, and his justifying himself therein against those who were offended at his doing it on that day, ver. 1-6. II. A lesson of humility gives to those who were ambitious of the highest rooms, ver. 7-11. III. A lesson of charity to those who feasted the rich, and did not feed the poor, ver. 12-14. IV.
14.s: Choosing the Seats at the Feast
14.i: Luke 14 takes place at a dinner table, where Jesus heals, teaches about seats and guests, and tells of a feast whose invited guests would not come.
14.p: Lord, You invite the poor and the overlooked to Your table. Make us people who open the door wide. Amen.
14.l: At lunch or at play today, pick the person who is usually left out and make room for them.
q: Jesus healed quietly so as neither to advertise himself nor provoke others. When does quiet service do more than a show?

15.o: Evil manners, we say, beget good laws; so, in this chapter, the murmuring of the scribes and Pharisees at the grace of Christ, and the favour he showed to publicans and sinners, gave occasion for a more full discovery of that grace than perhaps otherwise we should have had in these three parables which we have in this chapter, the scope of all of which is the same, to show, not only what God had said and sworn in the Old Testament, that he had no pleasure in the death and ruin of sinners, but that he had great…
15.i: When the Pharisees complained that Jesus welcomed sinners, He told two stories, of a lost sheep and a lost coin, about God's joy when one lost person is found.
15.p: Lord, thank You for looking for us until You find us. Teach us to rejoice when the lost come home. Amen.
15.l: If someone is left out or lost in a group today, go and find them. Invite them in and make them feel found.
q: God is like a shepherd and a woman who will not stop searching. Who is He searching for through you?

16.o: The scope of Christ's discourse in this chapter is to awaken and quicken us all so to use this world as not to abuse it, so to manage all our possessions and enjoyments here as that they may make for us, and may not make against us in the other world; for they will do either the one or the other, according as we use them now. I.
16.s: The Shrewd Manager and Lazarus at the Gate
16.i: Luke 16 pairs a puzzling story about a clever manager with the sharp story of a rich man and a beggar named Lazarus.
16.p: Lord, open our eyes to those at our gate. Teach us to use what You have given us to love people, and to listen to Your word. Amen.
16.l: Look for someone near you who needs help today, and do one thing for them before you do something for yourself.
q: People of this age plan ahead better than people of light. What are you planning for that will outlast this year?

17.o: In this chapter we have, I. Some particular discourses which Christ had with his disciples, in which he teaches them to take heed of giving offence, and to forgive the injuries done them (ver. 1-4), encourages them to pray for the increase of their faith (ver. 5, 6), and then teaches them humility, whatever service they had done for God, ver. 7-10. II. His cleansing ten lepers, and the thanks he had from one of them only, and he a Samaritan, ver. 11-19. III.
17.i: Jesus heals ten men with leprosy, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Him.
17.p: Lord Jesus, we thank You for all You have done. Help us to come back and give thanks. Amen.
17.l: Say thank you today to three people, and tell God thank you for something He did for you.
q: Nine were healed, and one returned to give thanks. What makes you stop and say thank you?

18.o: In this chapter we have, I. The parable of the importunate widow, designed to teach us fervency in prayer, ver. 1-8. II. The parable of the Pharisee and publican, designed to teach us humility, and humiliation for sin, in prayer, ver. 9-14. III. Christ's favour to little children that were brought to him, ver. 15-17. IV.
18.i: Luke 18 opens with the purpose of the story before it begins: Jesus tells this parable so that His followers will pray and not lose heart.
18.p: Lord, You are not like the unjust judge. Teach us to pray at all times and never lose heart. Amen.
18.l: Pray today about something you have stopped asking God for, and ask again.
q: What have you stopped praying about that you could bring to God again?

19.o: In this chapter we have, I. The conversion of Zaccheus the publican at Jericho, ver. 1-10. II. The parable of the pounds which the king entrusted with his servants, and of his rebellious citizens, ver. 11-27. III. Christ's riding in triumph (such triumph as it was) into Jerusalem; and his lamentation in prospect of the ruin of that city, ver. 28-44. IV. His teaching in the temple, and casting the buyers and sellers out of it, ver. 45-48.
19.i: Jesus invites himself to the house of the tax collector Zacchaeus, who gives away half his wealth.
19.p: Lord Jesus, You seek and save the lost. Come to our houses, and change our hearts. Amen.
19.l: Sit with someone today whom other people ignore, and be friendly to them.
q: The crowd grumbled when Jesus went to Zacchaeus's house. Whom do you tend to avoid?

20.o: In this chapter we have, I. Christ's answer to the chief priests' question concerning his authority, ver. 1-8. II. The parable of the vineyard let out to the unjust and rebellious husbandmen, ver. 9-19. III. Christ's answer to the question proposed to him concerning the lawfulness of paying tribute to Cæsar, ver. 20-26. IV. His vindication of that great fundamental doctrine of the Jewish and Christian institutes—the resurrection of the dead and the future state, from the foolish cavils of the Sadducees, ver. 27-38.
20.s: The Vineyard Tenants and the Coin
20.i: Luke 20 is a day of questions in the temple, from an angry challenge about authority to a trick question about tax.
20.p: Lord, everything belongs to You. Help us to give to You what is Yours, and to love the truth even when it is hard. Amen.
20.l: Look at a coin or a bill today, notice whose face is on it, and ask yourself what belongs to God in your own life.
q: The Herodians favored paying Caesar because their position depended on him. Whose approval is shaping your answers more than your convictions?

21.o: In this chapter we have, I. The notice Christ took, and the approbation he gave, of a poor widow that cast two mites into the treasury, ver. 1-4. II. A prediction of future events, in answer to his disciples' enquiries concerning them, ver. 5-7. 1. Of what should happen between that and the destruction of Jerusalem—false Christs arising, bloody wars and persecutions of Christ's followers, ver. 8-19. 2. Of that destruction itself, ver. 20-24. 3.
21.s: The Widow's Coins and the Signs
21.i: Luke 21 begins with a woman nobody noticed except Jesus, then turns to His warnings of what is coming.
21.p: Lord, You see what no one else sees. Teach us to give all of ourselves, and to stand with our heads up when the world shakes. Amen.
21.l: Give something small but real today, like your time, a toy, or a kind word, and give it with your whole heart.
q: Christ looked up to see what was given. What gift of yours has cost you something, whether or not anyone noticed?

22.o: All the evangelists, whatever they omit, give us a particular account of the death and resurrection of Christ, because he died for our sins and rose for our justification, this evangelist as fully as any, and with many circumstances and passages added which we had not before. In this chapter we have, I. The plot to take Jesus, and Judas's coming into it, ver. 1-6. II. Christ's eating the passover with his disciples, ver. 7-18. III. The instituting of the Lord's supper, ver. 19, 20. IV.
22.i: Luke 22 shows Jesus preparing the Passover meal with care, and then giving the bread and the cup a new meaning.
22.p: Lord Jesus, You gave Yourself for us. Help us to remember You whenever we eat and drink together. Amen.
22.l: Share a meal with someone today, and take a moment to thank God for it.
q: How might remembering Jesus change the way you sit down to an ordinary meal?

23.o: This chapter carries on and concludes the history of Christ's sufferings and death. We have here, I. His arraignment before Pilate the Roman governor, ver. 1-5. II. His examination before Herod, who was tetrarch of Galilee, under the Romans likewise, ver. 6-12. III. Pilate's struggle with the people to release Jesus, his repeated testimonies concerning his innocency, but his yielding at length to their importunity and condemning him to be crucified, ver. 13-25. IV.
23.i: On the cross Jesus forgave those who crucified Him, welcomed a dying man into paradise, and gave up His spirit, and a Roman officer said he was surely innocent.
23.p: Lord Jesus, thank You for the cross and for forgiving us. Help us to forgive, and to remember what it cost You. Amen.
23.l: Sit quietly for a minute today and thank Jesus for what He did on the cross.
q: Jesus forgave the people who crucified Him. Is there someone you are finding it hard to forgive?

24.o: Our Lord Jesus went gloriously down to death, in spite of the malice of his enemies, who did all they could to make his death ignominious; but he rose again more gloriously, of which we have an account in this chapter; and the proofs and evidences of Christ's resurrection are more fully related by this evangelist than they were by Matthew and Mark. Here is, I.
24.i: Two sad travelers walked and talked with the risen Jesus without knowing Him, until He broke bread at supper and they knew Him.
24.p: Lord Jesus, walk with us on our roads. Open the Scriptures to us, and be known to us in the breaking of the bread. Amen.
24.l: Today, invite someone to sit down with you for a meal or a snack, and really listen to what they have to say.
q: Their hearts burned while Jesus opened the Scriptures. When has something you heard made your heart burn?
